definition.text: Capturing energy produced at one time so it can be used later, which reduces imbalances between energy demand and supply.

facts.text: Storage means converting energy from forms that are hard to store into forms that are more convenient or cheaper to store.
Pumped-storage hydroelectricity is the largest-capacity form of active grid storage; EPRI reported in March 2012 that it accounts for over 99% of bulk storage capacity worldwide.
Pumped-storage efficiency varies in practice between 70% and 80%, with claims of up to 87%.

Other families include compressed air, flywheels, thermal storage, rechargeable and flow batteries, supercapacitors, and chemical routes such as power-to-gas turning electricity into hydrogen or methane.
To exceed 40% self-sufficiency in a household with photovoltaics, storage is needed.
Storage helps overcome the intermittency of renewable energy, but cost makes batteries impractical for the large storage needed to balance seasonal swings.
The economics depend on the reserve service requested and several uncertain factors, so the best storage size is market and location dependent.

definition.text: Both a structure and the processes that make it environmentally responsible and resource-efficient across its life cycle, from planning to demolition.

facts.text: As of 2020 buildings account for 37% of global energy use and energy-related CO2 emissions; counting the manufacture of building materials, the share is 39%.
UNEP warns that without new construction technologies emissions from buildings could double by 2050.

Life cycle assessment covers all cradle-to-grave impacts, such as embodied energy, global warming potential, resource use, pollution and waste; it is the best way to evaluate buildings but is not yet a consistent requirement of rating systems.
As buildings use less operating energy, embodied energy can reach as much as 30% of life cycle energy consumption.
Most green buildings cost a premium of under 2% but yield 10 times as much over the building's life.
The most criticized issue is price, since photovoltaics, new appliances and modern technologies tend to cost more.
Rating systems such as BREEAM (UK), LEED (US and Canada), DGNB (Germany), CASBEE (Japan) and GRIHA (India) help consumers judge a structure's environmental level.
